paragraphs.heading: What an outcome is
paragraphs.text: In probability, an outcome is one possible result of an experiment or trial. Different outcomes are mutually exclusive, so only one of them happens on each trial. All the possible outcomes together make up the sample space.

paragraphs.heading: Two coin flips
paragraphs.text: Flip a coin twice and there are four possible outcomes: (H, T), (T, H), (T, T) and (H, H). Here H stands for heads and T for tails. Those four outcomes form the sample space of this experiment.

paragraphs.heading: Outcomes versus events
paragraphs.text: Outcomes are not the same as events, which are sets, or groups, of outcomes. In the two-flip experiment, the event "at least one heads" contains every outcome except (T, T). Outcomes get grouped into events because single outcomes may matter little in practice, or because there may be far too many of them, even infinitely many. An event with exactly one outcome is an elementary event, the event holding every outcome is the sample space itself, and one outcome can sit in many events.

paragraphs.heading: How likely an outcome is
paragraphs.text: Outcomes can have probabilities anywhere from zero to one, inclusive. In a discrete distribution with a finite sample space, each outcome gets its own probability. In a continuous distribution, every single outcome has probability zero, and only ranges of outcomes can have non-zero probability. Some mixed distributions combine continuous stretches with discrete outcomes, called atoms, and these atoms can have non-zero probability.

paragraphs.heading: Equally likely outcomes
paragraphs.text: In some sample spaces it makes sense to assume every outcome is equally likely. For an ordinary coin, heads and tails are typically taken as equally likely. Most randomizing tools in games of chance, such as dice, shuffled cards, spinning wheels and drawing lots, quietly rely on this assumption, and players who cheat may try to bend it with marked cards or loaded dice. Not every experiment works this way: toss a thumb tack, and no symmetry suggests that point-up and point-down should be equally likely.
